The basic e}ects observed for the 19 CrÐ14 Ni "3[4 Mo# steels investigated here are that nitrogen increases pitting corrosion resistance\ and depresses both active dissolution and passive current densities[ These \_ndings are in agreement with the majority of reported investigations and de\_ne the basic framework which must be covered by any proposed mechanism for the nitrogen e}ect[ In addition\ there are two further e}ects which are apparent in several of the investigations performed here and which per se provide mechanistically useful information[ The \_rst is that nitrogen enhances repassivation[ This is apparent in the pitting potential measurements\ in that the potential for the initiation of the \_rst pits is similar for both low! and high! nitrogen steels but repeated repassivation of pits in the latter case leads to a higher \_nal breakdown potential[ Similarly\ nitrogen also reduces the magnitude of the subcritical depassivation events\ apparent as transients during passive current density measurements[ The second major e}ect is that of MoÐN synergism[ This is apparent in the CPT results\ also in the passive current density measurements and the polarisation curves in acidic solution[ During the passive current density measurements\ mol! ybdenum appreciably reduces the number of depassivation events\ as evidenced by current transients\ while Mo and N in combination e}ectively eliminate these tran! sients[ Polarisation curves also show that the bene\_cial e}ect of nitrogen in reducing active dissolution is retained to lower critical current densities in the presence of molybdenum[

On the basis of thermodynamics ð63Ł\ ammonium is the stable species at low potentials and $\mathrm { p H }$ "such as occur in pits and crevices# but nitrate should dominate at high potentials[ However\ the solution analyses after dissolution under active\ pitting and transpassive dissolution conditions Fig[ 01 demonstrate unequivocally that $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } ^ { + } }$ is the dominant dissolution product of the nitrogen in solid solution in the steel[ This indicates that reaction kinetics rather than thermodynamics are of overriding importance in the electrochemistry of nitrogen dissolution[ However\ it does not provide any indication of the surface reaction taking place[ Equations "0\ 1 and 4# all result in $\mathrm { N H } _ { 3 } / \mathrm { N H } _ { 4 } ^ { + }$ formation\ but make di}erent assumptions about the state of the surface nitrogen prior to dissolution[ Equation "0# is cathodic and thus should slow down as the potential is raised[ In contrast\ eq[ "1# and eq[ "4# are potential independent in that they involve a reduced form of nitrogen "nitride or $\mathbf { N } ^ { 3 - } )$ on the surface\ and are thus more probable candidates for ammonium formation under a wide range of conditions[ This aspect is discussed further in Section 3[1\ on surface segregation\ below[

This dominant presence of NH<sup>¦</sup><sub>3</sub> after dissolution e}ectively excludes a nitrate! based mechanism[ At high potentials\ a nitrate mechanism would require that the thermodynamically stable $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ be reduced to the $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } ^ { + } }$ which is detected[ A mech! anism whereby NH<sup>¦</sup> is formed initially and then oxidised to $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ with an inhibiting function "see Section 0[3# is likewise excluded as this would require the process $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } ^ { + } } \mathrm {  N O _ { 3 } ^ { - } } \mathrm {  N H _ { 4 } ^ { + } }$ to occur[ Further convincing evidence that NH<sup>¦</sup> is the critical species has been supplied by the elegant work of Kim et al[ ð64Ł[ They exposed pure Cr in nitrate!containing solutions at various potentials and demonstrated with XPS that nitrate was reduced to $\mathrm { N H } _ { 3 } / \mathrm { N H } _ { 4 } ^ { + }$ over the potential range from −829 to $+ 1 3 0 0 \mathrm { m V } \mathrm { S C E } ,$ \ also that reduction to a surface nitride could occur when the passive \_lm was absent "at low potential# or damaged "high potential#[ This again contradicts the thermodynamic data and again indicates that nitrogen in stainless steels does not oxidise to $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$

3[1[ Surface se\`re\`ation

One question in terms of surface segregation which is open to critical evaluation is the suggestion by Newman and Shahrabi ð1Ł\ detailed in Section 0[6\ that anodic segregation of nitrogen may block surface dissolution sites and thereby cause quasi! passivation[ Information in this context is provided by the electrochemical behaviour in acidic chloride solutions[ These environments are of particular interest because they approximate to conditions prevailing during propagating pitting or crevice cor! rosion[ At all the concentrations investigated here\ 9[1 to 5 M HCl\ there was no evidence of salt \_lm formation prior to passivation[ This is in notable contrast to the work of the aforementioned authors ð1Ł in which borderline conditions were identi\_ed where a 06 CrÐ01 NiÐ1[4 Mo steel exhibited salt \_lm formation\ but the corresponding alloy with 9[11) N exhibited reversible passivation

In the present investigation\ the passivation process was found to be the same for both low and high nitrogen steels[ In less aggressive environments\ passivation proceeded when the potential sweep direction was reversed from the anodic to the cathodic direction just after passing the active dissolution peak while\ in more con! centrated HCl solutions\ reversible passivation occurred Fig[ 6[ Although reversible passivation may\ in some cases\ be attributable to surface nitrogen accumulation\ as suggested by Newman and Shahrabi ð1Ł\ this is clearly not the case in the alloy systems investigated here[ The observed e}ects are instead consistent with conventional pas! sivation by oxide \_lm formation[ A second observation which argues against the hypothesis that sluggish nitrogen dissolution causes kink site blockage due to nitrogen accumulation is that of impedance measurements[ There is no indication in the impedance measurements of any additional time constant which can be related to the presence of nitrogen in the steel[ Thus there is no support for the idea that eq[ "0# has become the rate determining step for dissolution of the entire alloy[ On the contrary\ it appears that nitrogen only causes slight modi\_cation of the impedance parameters relating to dissolution of other alloy components and to passive \_lm formation[ However\ the impedance results do not exclude the possibility of surface nitrogen bonding which limits dissolution of all species

The issue of whether surface segregation is occurring to any extent is more di.cult to treat on the basis of electrochemical measurements alone[ However\ at least one observation in the present study cannot be readily explained only by solution chem! istry e}ects\ namely that nitrogen decreased the passive current density so less charge was requires for passive \_lm formation[ A parallel may be drawn to the e}ect of increasing levels of Cr on the passive current density for FeÐCr alloys ð60Ł[ Whether this e}ect of nitrogen is attributable to a decrease in \_lm thickness or to an alteration in \_lm:surface properties cannot be ascertained from the available data\ but it is clearly not related to ammonium formation in that a negligible amount of dissolution is taking place[ A possible explanation is provided by the concept of surface nitrogen accumulation[ Ample evidence for nitrogen enrichment beneath the passive \_lm has been supplied by surface analytical investigations\ as detailed in Section 0[5\ and such an e}ect may well explain the present results[ Molybdenum alloying appears to have a di}erent e}ect on passive \_lm growth since it decreases the gradient of the log"i#Ð log"t# plots in Fig[ 4[ As discussed by Kirchheim ð65Ł\ this may be due to a larger amount of dissolution occurring during passive \_lm formation or to changes in di}usivity within the \_lm[ The speci\_c observation of Marshall and Burstein ð66Ł that molybdenum raises the electric \_eld over the \_lm and thereby promotes dissolution of the iron component during the early stages of \_lm formation on scratched elec! trodes\ may also be of relevance\ even though the increased charge that they observed to be associated with passivation in molybdenum!alloyed steels is not apparent at the longer times investigated here[

If\ on the basis of the convincing body of evidence in the literature\ it is accepted that surface segregation of nitrogen does occur to some extent\ then several forms of nitrogen are possible[ Segregated atomic nitrogen\ negatively charged nitrogen and a nitride phase have variously been suggested[ The interfacial compositions evaluated by Olefjord and Wegrelius ð36Ł\ using variable angle XPS\ correspond to a nitrogen content in the sub\_lm monolayer of 2Ð5 wt[)\ the corresponding value from the AES investigation of Lu et al[ ð45Ł is 2)[ These values are within the range of typical nitrogen contents in nitrides "e[g[ 01) in $\mathrm { C r } _ { 2 } \mathrm { N } .$ \ 4) in h phase\ 0[4) in p!phase ð67Ł# so nitride bonding "or at least a negatively charged nitrogen species# appears more probable than either atomic nitrogen enrichment in solid solution or surface inter! metallic phase formation[ Much of the XPS evidence detailed in Section 0 also points to negatively charged surface nitrogen species[ Obviously\ no evidence for the form of surface segregated nitrogen can be provided by the present electrochemical inves! tigation\ but it can be pointed out that the presence of a reduced form of nitrogen in the metallic state is more compatible with the observed ammonium formation\ since the latter can then be attributed to eq[ "1# or eq[ "4#[ Equation "0#\ in contrast\ is a cathodic reaction and thus di.cult to reconcile with observations of ammonium at high potentials[

Another interesting e}ect of mechanistic signi\_cance in this context is the range over which nitrogen a}ects the critical current density[ For the Mo!free K series of steels\ a bene\_cial e}ect of nitrogen on active dissolution is just apparent in 0 M $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 } + 0 . 5$ M HCl\ in which the critical current densities are around $1 0 \mathrm { m A } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ while\ at a lower HCl concentration\ a slight detrimental e}ect is observed instead[ In contrast\ for the Mo!alloyed L series of steels\ the bene\_cial e}ect is still apparent in 0M $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 } + 0 . 2 \mathrm { M }$ HCl at critical current densities just above $1 0 \mu \mathrm { A } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ [ These current densities correspond to charges of $3 { \mathrm { C } } / { \mathrm { c m } } ^ { 2 }$ and $3 \mathrm { m C } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ and thus the dis! solution of approximately 4999 and 4 atomic layers respectively[ One possible expla! nation of this behaviour is that molybdenum enhances surface retention of nitrogen[ For both CrÐNi and CrÐNiÐMo steels\ the bene\_cial e}ect of nitrogen on active dissolution disappears in more aggressive solutions\ at critical current densities of the order of 0 $\mathbf { A } / \mathbf { c m } ^ { 2 } .$ [ It may be that the NH<sup>¦</sup> e}ect is insu.cient to bu}er even the near! surface pH if the solution becomes su.ciently aggressive\ but this e}ect may also be related to surface segregation and interaction[

In summary\ although a number of proposed mechanisms for the e}ect of nitrogen on corrosion resistance can be excluded as explanations for the e}ects observed in the present study\ there are several mechanisms that appear to be relevant and are probably acting simultaneously[ Surface nitrogen accumulation and an altered surface bonding state\ possibly approximating to nitride formation\ are important[ pH bu}! ering by $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } ^ { + } }$ formation\ probably from a nitride or negatively charged nitrogen state\ as described in eq[ "1# or eq[ "4#\ is also of signi\_cance[ However\ the relative importance of the e}ects is still an open question and may depend on the speci\_c dissolution condition under investigation[
